column3: It explicitly presents sons within divinely extended material support, directly echoing the focus premise.
The final recompense and rapid account correct any present-world inference drawn from possessions.
Its mention of the Children of Israel concerns release from Pharaoh, not wealth, sons, or their interpretation.
Wealth and sons function as the worldly status behind arrogant rejection, matching the focus's suspect inference.
The nearby Mosaic gift continues the surah's contrast between guidance and complacent reception of gifts.
It directly joins extended provision to wealth and sons, though here it is promised in response to repentance.
It exposes the false belief that accumulated wealth guarantees permanence, a precise form of the focus's error.
The immediately preceding verse names the heedlessness in which the focus question leaves them.
Extended wealth is explicitly given as a favor yet becomes part of an ungrateful recipient's case.
It repeats extension through wealth and sons, while its military restoration prevents wealth from proving final favor.
It regulates stewardship of wealth but does not address extended provision as evidence of divine approval.
It rejects the inference that delayed judgment means divine neglect, closely parallel to the focus's question.
It states that wealth and sons fail at the decisive judgment, directly limiting their apparent present value.
Its call for sound provision and righteous action supplies the local alternative to reading provision as approval.
It again forbids treating delay as failure of the divine promise, reinforcing the correction of superficial judgment.
It forbids fixation on others' temporary enjoyment, a practical response to the allure questioned in the focus.
The nearby record and non-injustice establish a measured judgment beyond visible distributions of wealth.
The shared extension language describes the punishment's pillars rather than provision or a mistaken reading of it.
Sons are part of the granted advantages surrounding the recipient whose response is condemned.
Divine counting of every person relativizes the security supposedly supplied by family or possessions.
The root overlap is about building the sky, not children or the significance of worldly provision.
It assigns the final account to God, directly countering judgments based solely on present prosperity.
The immediate call to one community and God-consciousness supplies the surah's normative frame for the focus.
It illustrates that what observers think they see can be false, though its scene is not about provision.
Its rhetorical question rebukes a false assumption about purposelessness and return, closely matching the focus's form.
It resumes the same state of heedless hearts that explains why recipients misread their situation.
It concerns the polemical allocation of daughters and sons to God and people, not material favor.
Its language of one sea extending another contrasts finite visible supply with the inexhaustibility of God's words.
It explicitly tells people to recognize known abundance as provision extended by God rather than self-sufficiency.
Their refusal to expect an account identifies the future judgment that present prosperity can obscure.
Even all earthly wealth cannot ransom its possessors, and unforeseen judgment overturns their calculations.
The local description of factions delighted with what they possess helps explain complacent misreading of gifts.
Gathering and counting wealth becomes the basis for the same false security exposed in the following verse.
It treats wealth as a means for manumission and justice, without the focus's question about its meaning.
The nearby faithful give while fearing return to God, a direct contrast to complacent confidence in provision.
It concerns spending wealth and selves in striving, not interpreting prosperity as divine endorsement.
The formula overlap is incidental; the verse is a general proclamation and warning.
The immediately nearby fear of the Lord contrasts sharply with the focus recipients' unperceiving confidence.
Solomon rejects wealth offered as leverage and distinguishes divine gift from human material patronage.
The objection concerns material expectations for a messenger, not extended wealth and children as a sign of favor.
It begins Noah's call in the same surah but supplies no specific provision or false-inference relation.
Its reference to the Children of Israel is genealogical and unrelated to the focus theme.
The formula occurrence concerns judgment by revelation, not the interpretation of prosperity.
This immediate-surah affirmation of belief marks the faithful orientation opposed to heedless misperception.
It explicitly denies that a person's wealth can save them at their fall, undermining wealth as security.
The verse concerns following desire after rejecting revelation; its formula overlap is not thematic.
This local messenger narrative lacks a direct connection to wealth, children, or their apparent meaning.
It recasts wealth as something given away for purification rather than proof of privileged standing.
Universal divine possession and accounting place personal wealth beneath a fuller judgment of what people conceal.
It depicts condemned criminals in chains without a specific link to provision or mistaken prosperity.
The sons comparison concerns certainty of recognition, not wealth and children as worldly favor.
It directly says wealth and earnings do not avail their owner, denying their presumed protective force.
This immediately adjacent rejection of association identifies the theological failure beneath misreading gifts.
It treats wealth as a resource for struggle, not as evidence from which divine approval is inferred.
It describes continuously renewed provision, but in a rewarded afterlife scene rather than deceptive worldly abundance.
The Moses and Aaron narrative is local context but has no direct relation to the focus question.
Its rhetorical correction of what people should regard as remarkable parallels the focus's correction of an assumption.
It says God extends worldly giving to both groups, making such provision unsuitable evidence of final favor.
It explicitly calls wealth and children a test, directly replacing the focus recipients' favorable reading.
The phrase concerns sending the Children of Israel away, not children as a granted worldly resource.
It nearly restates the focus logic: unbelievers must not think the time extended to them is for their good.
The local punishment of the affluent shows that luxury does not secure recipients from reversal.
Sons appear in a prayer for protection from idolatry, not as evidence of prosperous favor.
God's lack of need for provision establishes Him as giver rather than a beneficiary of human resources.
Noah's request for a blessed landing is local context without the focus's evaluative theme.
The daughters reference serves a narrative intervention and has no wealth or extension relation.
Extension here is punishment rather than favor, showing that continued allowance cannot be read as good.
The verse gives wisdom and calls for gratitude, without a specific relation to wealth, children, or delay.
The Children of Israel are cited as knowledgeable witnesses, not as beneficiaries of wealth or offspring.
It rebukes the assumption that hidden speech escapes God, structurally paralleling the focus's false supposition.
The immediate refusal of help after punishment exposes the fragility of the recipients' prior security.
Its inheritance by the Children of Israel is a historical reversal, not an interpretation of wealth and children.
Those diverted from the path nonetheless think themselves guided, a close analogue to the focus's unperceived error.
The local question about rejecting a known messenger adds to the surah's diagnosis of willful denial.
It names the rescue of the Children of Israel but does not engage the focus's material-provision theme.
God's extension within rebellion shows that continued scope can expose and deepen error rather than reward it.
Reward beyond reckoning contrasts divine valuation with calculations based on immediately visible goods.
It disputes a false preference for daughters or sons in an attribution to God, not worldly prosperity.
Evil companions continually extend misguidance, a negative analogue to extension whose apparent continuation is not good.
The verse immediately answers the focus question: they do not perceive that this is not hastening good for them.
Sons occur in an eschatological scene of flight from family, without an extension or prosperity inference.
It defines Satan's authority over his allies, with no meaningful connection to wealth, children, or delay.
Each person comes alone at resurrection, limiting the ultimate security of family and accumulated support.
It concerns transmitting religious commitment to sons rather than evaluating material gifts.
The formula is part of a rejection charge and does not concern the focus's themes.
The immediate contrast is exact: believers hasten in good works, rather than merely receiving imagined good.
It regulates principal wealth after repentance, not provision as a sign of divine favor.
The formula concerns the timing of threatened punishment and has no direct wealth or children link.
The instruction not to hasten them because they are being counted supports the theme of delayed but measured reckoning.
It rebukes another false supposition that created servants can be adopted as protectors against God.
The punitive image has no substantive relation to wealth, sons, extension, or a false inference.
A person mistakes a mirage for water before meeting God's account, vividly paralleling deceptive confidence and correction.
It records rejection of a reminder without addressing the focus's material or temporal premise.
The nearby provision of secure shelter and flowing water belongs to the surah's gift-and-guidance setting.
The promised Day of Account supplies the future horizon that prevents present abundance from being decisive.
It condemns treating a grave matter as trivial, another clear case of an apparently plausible but false evaluation.
Its denial that food relieves hunger provides a narrow analogue to material provision failing its assumed benefit.
Fortified people miscalculate their security and are struck from an unforeseen direction, directly challenging worldly confidence.
It announces guidance and success without a specific relationship to provision, children, or mistaken calculation.
It rejects the assumption that wrongdoers and faithful people share equal outcomes, matching the focus's critique of false inference.
It directly denies that wealth and children can protect disbelievers from God, overturning their presumed security.
It names wealth and sons among the attractive adornments of worldly life, supplying the allure behind the focus's misreading.
It repeats that wealth and children will not avail their possessors before God.
It explicitly makes wealth and persons a field of testing, qualifying any simple reading of abundance as favor.
The opening of every worldly benefit to those who forgot the warning ends in sudden seizure, a central prosperity-as-trial parallel.
God's granting of respite to wrongdoers shows that extended time is not evidence of approval.
It explicitly forbids admiration of their wealth and children because these become a means of punishment in worldly life.
It recalls earlier communities with greater wealth and children whose enjoyment did not prevent their ruin.
It repeats the warning not to be impressed by wealth and children, directly reinforcing 9:55.
Moses identifies Pharaoh's splendor and wealth as a worldly test that contributes to others' misguidance.
It promises good provision only within repentance and obedience, distinguishing provision from unconditional endorsement.
Those seeking worldly life are repaid there in full, yet that visible repayment does not establish their final good.
It states the hereafter's loss for people whose worldly gains are exhausted there, correcting temporal calculation.
God expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in worldly life despite its limited relation to the hereafter.
A secure and well-provisioned town loses its favors through ingratitude, showing abundance to be contingent rather than confirmatory.
The giver expands and restricts provision by knowledge, making worldly allocation an unsuitable final verdict on a person.
Satan's promised share in wealth and children presents these goods as a sphere of temptation rather than simple blessing.
It forbids turning one's eyes toward people who desire worldly adornment, closely matching the focus on misleading visible prosperity.
The parable introduces unequal gardens and wealth as the setting for a false confidence about worldly endowment.
The garden owner boasts of greater wealth and a stronger following, directly joining possessions to mistaken status.
He enters his garden assuming it will never perish, the same false permanence inferred from prosperity.
The destruction of the garden leaves its owner regretting his expenditure, overturning the security claimed through wealth.
It explicitly calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life while ranking enduring good works above them.
It forbids extending one's gaze toward others' worldly splendor because it is a test, not a final good.
Good and evil are both named as tests, providing the general principle that pleasant provision is also evaluative.
Whatever people receive is described as temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.
Qarun's wealth leads him to exult and deny its proper moral meaning, a narrative embodiment of the focus's error.
Qarun attributes his wealth to personal knowledge, directly opposing recognition that provision is extended by God.
Observers desire Qarun's worldly portion, displaying the attraction of prosperity before its reversal.
Qarun's sudden swallowing shows that exceptional wealth cannot secure its owner from divine reversal.
The alternation of expanded and restricted provision is offered as a sign, not as a simple measure of worth.
The boast of greater wealth and children is explicitly coupled with the false claim that punishment will not reach them.
It corrects that boast by saying God expands and restricts provision, though most people do not know.
It expressly denies that wealth and children bring people near to God, making it one of the clearest omitted parallels.
A recipient of bounty calls it personal knowledge, then the verse identifies the bounty as a test that most fail to recognize.
God's expansion and restriction of provision is presented as a sign for believers, limiting status-based inference.
It again locates expanded and restricted provision in divine control rather than human deservingness.
Its distribution of livelihood and ranks makes worldly allotment a divinely ordered condition, not proof of superior favor.
It rebukes people who consumed their good things in worldly life, exposing the loss behind apparently successful enjoyment.
It characterizes worldly life as rivalry in wealth and children and compares its growth to vegetation that soon decays.
It warns believers not to let wealth and children distract them from God's remembrance, identifying their spiritual danger.
It explicitly calls wealth and children a trial and directs attention to the greater reward with God.
God's respite to deniers is paired with an inescapable plan, directly qualifying prolonged ease as favorable.
On the Day of Judgment, a wrongdoer would offer his sons as ransom, showing their inability to provide real security.
The passage begins with the man whom God made wealthy and provided for, framing later condemnation of his response.
God says He made the recipient's circumstances smooth, making his wealth and sons an extended ease rather than self-made proof.
His demand for further increase after such gifts displays the entitlement that the focus interrogates.
It explicitly records the human inference that generous provision means divine honor.
Its paired correction shows that restricted provision does not mean humiliation, establishing the exact evaluative contrast.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts until death, identifying wealth-driven comparison as spiritually deceptive.
